title: The Kirtland Safety Society: An Illegal Bank Backed by Claimed Revelation
claim: In November 1836 Joseph Smith co-founded the Kirtland Safety Society bank; when the Ohio legislature denied a charter, it reorganized in January 1837 as the 'Kirtland Safety Society Anti-Banking Company' and issued notes anyway. On January 6, 1837, Wilford Woodruff recorded in his journal that Smith declared he had 'receieved that morning the word of the Lord upon the subject of the Kirtland Safety Society' — 'not ownly the voice of the spirit... but even an audaible voice' — and that if the commandments were heeded 'all would be well.' Warren Parrish, an officer of the bank who later left the church, claimed Smith prophesied it would 'like Aaron's rod... swallow up all other banks... and survive when all others should be laid in ruins.' The bank was massively undercapitalized; its notes lost most value within weeks. On October 24, 1837, Smith and Rigdon were each fined $1,000 plus costs for illegal banking (Rounds qui tam v. Smith, under Ohio's 1816 statute). Smith fled Kirtland the night of January 12, 1838. Historians estimate 200-300 members (roughly 10-15% of Kirtland membership, including about a third of general church leadership) left the church in the fallout; Heber C. Kimball later said that at the time, for every member who stood by Joseph Smith as prophet, 'there were twenty who did not.'

Transcript of Proceedings, Rounds qui tam v. Rigdon/Smith, Oct 1837 (Joseph Smith Papers)
Introduction to the Kirtland Safety Society (Joseph Smith Papers)
Church History Topics: Kirtland Safety Society (LDS Church)
Warren Parrish letter, Painesville Republican, 15 Feb 1838 (repr. UTLM)

Walker, 'The Kirtland Safety Society and the Fraud of Grandison Newell' (BYU Studies)

response: FAIR and church historians argue: (1) the 1830s was the era of unregulated 'wildcat' banking, and hundreds of banks — many chartered — failed in the national Panic of 1837, so the KSS collapse reflects the economy, not fraud; (2) the charter denial owed to Ohio legislative politics (hard-money Democrats denied nearly all new charters that session, and anti-Mormon sentiment may have contributed), and operating as a joint-stock 'anti-banking' company followed legal counsel's advice under genuinely unsettled law; (3) Joseph Smith invested more of his own money than almost anyone and lost heavily — the opposite of a fraudster's profile; (4) Smith resigned in June 1837 and publicly warned the Saints against the notes before the worst of the collapse; (5) Woodruff's journal does not record the content of the claimed revelation, and the grandiose 'swallow up all banks' prophecy comes only from Warren Parrish, by then a hostile ex-member with his own alleged role in the bank's failure.

responseSource.name: FAIR: Creation of the Kirtland Safety Society

rationale: The load-bearing facts are conceded in the church's own publications: the Joseph Smith Papers and the Church History Topics essay acknowledge the charter denial, the decision to operate anyway, the October 1837 fines for illegal banking, Smith's flight to Missouri, and that leaders bore responsibility for 'failing to anticipate problems.' The revelation claim rests not on hostile sources but on the faithful, contemporaneous Woodruff journal published by the church-affiliated Woodruff Papers Project — Smith attached 'the word of the Lord' and an 'audible voice' to an enterprise that failed within months, was ruled illegal, and triggered the largest apostasy of his lifetime. The steelman genuinely mitigates intent (fraud is not established; the Panic of 1837 was real; Parrish's version deserves discounting as hostile) but does not touch the core problem under Deut 18:21-22: a claimed divine assurance ('all would be well') that events falsified. Severity tempered only in that the specific revelation's full wording was never recorded, so the strongest 'prophecy' framing depends partly on Parrish.

title: Post-Manifesto Polygamy (1890-1904): Public Denial, Private Practice — the Second Time
claim: The 1890 Manifesto (Official Declaration 1) publicly announced the end of plural marriage, and church leaders repeatedly denied any new plural marriages thereafter. In fact, apostles and members of the First Presidency secretly authorized or performed roughly 250 new plural marriages between 1890 and 1904 (D. Michael Quinn, 'LDS Church Authority and New Plural Marriages, 1890-1904,' Dialogue 18:1, 1985; B. Carmon Hardy's Solemn Covenant appendix documents 262), many in Mexico, Canada, and at sea; nine or ten General Authorities themselves took new plural wives. The Reed Smoot Senate hearings (1904-1907) exposed the practice: church president Joseph F. Smith testified under oath in March 1904 that he had continued to cohabit with his five plural wives and had fathered eleven children with them since 1890, in acknowledged violation of the law. Weeks later he issued the 1904 Second Manifesto — while asserting no post-1890 marriages had occurred 'with the sanction, consent or knowledge of the Church,' a claim contradicted by the documented participation of his own counselors and apostles. Apostles John W. Taylor and Matthias F. Cowley were forced from the Quorum of the Twelve over the affair. This repeats the Nauvoo pattern (1841-1844), when Joseph Smith and other leaders publicly denied polygamy while privately practicing it — making 1890-1904 the second sustained episode of institutional public denial of a privately continued practice.

sources.name: D. Michael Quinn, 'LDS Church Authority and New Plural Marriages, 1890-1904,' Dialogue 18:1 (1985): 9-105
Reed Smoot hearings, testimony of Joseph F. Smith (Proceedings, U.S. Senate Committee on Privileges and Elections, 1904, vol. 1; transcript excerpts)
Gospel Topics essay: 'The Manifesto and the End of Plural Marriage' (LDS Church)
B. Carmon Hardy, Solemn Covenant: The Mormon Polygamous Passage (Univ. of Illinois Press, 1992) — BYU Studies review
1904 Second Manifesto statement (BYU-Idaho archives)
Church History Topics: Reed Smoot Hearings (LDS Church)

response: The church's own Gospel Topics essay supplies the steelman and concedes most of the record: 'After October 1890, plural marriages continued to be quietly performed' in Mexico and Canada; 'The Manifesto declared President Woodruff's intention to submit to the laws of the United States. It said nothing about the laws of other nations' — so leaders in good faith read it as a legally-scoped document, not a revelation banning the principle worldwide; 'many Church leaders believed the Manifesto merely suspended plural marriage for an indefinite time'; existing husbands 'continued to cohabit with their plural wives and fathered children with them well into the 20th century' rather than abandon covenant families; and only with the 1904 Second Manifesto were members 'put on notice that new plural marriages stood unapproved by God and the Church,' after which Taylor and Cowley 'were eventually dropped from the quorum.' Apologists add that the transition away from a practice leaders believed divinely commanded was wrenching, conducted under federal persecution, and that ambiguity — not coordinated conspiracy — explains the fifteen-year lag.

responseSource.name: Gospel Topics essay: The Manifesto and the End of Plural Marriage

rationale: This is the rare case where the church's own essay concedes nearly every element of the critical claim: post-Manifesto plural marriages quietly performed with leader involvement, continued cohabitation and child-fathering, the Manifesto's deliberately limited legal scope, and the removal of two apostles. Joseph F. Smith's sworn Smoot testimony is a first-person presidential admission. What the steelman reframes — sincere ambiguity versus duplicity — cannot erase that leaders publicly and repeatedly denied what they privately authorized (including the Second Manifesto's 'sanction, consent or knowledge' claim, falsified by Quinn's and Hardy's documentation), and that this replays the Nauvoo denial pattern. Under the biblical standard of Prov 12:22 and Eph 4:25 the institutional pattern of public denial during private practice stands conceded in substance, contested only in motive.

title: Facsimile 1: 'Abraham on the Altar' vs. a Standard Embalming/Resurrection Vignette
claim: Joseph Smith published Facsimile 1 as Abraham 'fastened upon an altar' with 'the idolatrous priest of Elkenah attempting to offer up Abraham as a sacrifice' (Facsimile 1 Explanation, figs. 2-3; cf. Abraham 1:12-15). Egyptology identifies the original — extant as Papyrus Joseph Smith I, part of the Book of Breathings made for the Theban priest Hor (Ptolemaic era, ~2nd-1st century BC, some 1,500+ years after Abraham) — as a standard funerary lion-couch vignette: the jackal-headed god Anubis attending the deceased Osiris/Hor. The papyrus has a lacuna (missing section) exactly where the priest's head and alleged knife appear in the 1842 published version; the woodcut restoration shows a bald human head and a drawn knife, while Egyptologists (Ritner and others) note ink traces of a headdress at the shoulder indicating a jackal-headed Anubis, and no parallel vignette shows a knife. Smith's restoration and his identifications (bird as 'Angel of the Lord,' canopic jars as idolatrous gods of foreign nations, crocodile as 'idolatrous god of Pharaoh') do not match any accepted Egyptological reading.

sources.name: Robert K. Ritner, The Joseph Smith Egyptian Papyri: A Complete Edition (2013); 'The Breathing Permit of Hor' (JNES 62, 2003) — summarized with translations
Gospel Topics essay: 'Translation and Historicity of the Book of Abraham' (LDS Church)
FAIR: Book of Abraham facsimiles — missing portions of Facsimile 1
Pearl of Great Price Central: 'The Idolatrous Priest (Facsimile 1, Figure 3)'
Book of Abraham Facsimile 1 analysis (4witness)

response: Gee, Muhlestein, and Pearl of Great Price Central argue: (1) the lacuna means no one knows what the original showed — some apologists contend the papyrus was already damaged in 1835 and that a knife and human head could have stood there, noting this vignette is unusual among lion-couch scenes (the figure on the couch appears alive, clothed, with both hands possibly raised); (2) there is Egyptian evidence for ritual slaying of enemies in temple contexts, so a 'sacrifice' reading is not absurd; (3) on the 'Semitic adaptation' theory, ancient Jews in Egypt demonstrably reused and reinterpreted Egyptian iconography (e.g., the Demotic 'Abraham' connection in later magical papyri), so the vignette could have served as an illustration for an Abraham text regardless of its funerary origin; (4) the Book of Abraham may be a revealed text for which the papyri were merely a catalyst, making the facsimile explanations inspired commentary rather than Egyptological translation.

responseSource.name: Pearl of Great Price Central: The Idolatrous Priest (Facsimile 1, Figure 3)

rationale: Unlike Facsimiles 2 and 3, Facsimile 1 contains a genuine evidentiary gap: the lacuna covers precisely the disputed elements (priest's head, knife), so the restoration argument runs on parallels and ink traces rather than a surviving original. The scholarly consensus — Anubis in a routine embalming/resurrection scene from Hor's Breathing Permit — is far better supported (headdress traces, hundreds of parallel vignettes, zero parallels with a knife), and the church's own essay concedes Egyptologists' readings differ from Smith's. But because apologists dispute what filled the lacuna rather than the Egyptology itself, and the vignette does have unusual features, this figure-level claim is scored contested rather than unrefuted — while noting the surrounding identifications (canopic jars as foreign gods, crocodile as Pharaoh's god) find no Egyptological support at all.

title: Facsimile 2, Figure 7: The Fertility God Min as 'God Sitting upon His Throne'
claim: Facsimile 2 is a hypocephalus (a funerary amulet placed under a mummy's head, from Book of the Dead spell 162, made for one Sheshonq) — a well-understood class of object meant to keep the deceased warm and aid resurrection. Joseph Smith's explanations instead present it as cosmology: fig. 1 as 'Kolob, signifying the first creation, nearest to the celestial, or the residence of God,' fig. 5 as the sun receiving light 'through the medium of Kae-e-vanrash,' etc. Most starkly, figure 7 — which Egyptologists uniformly identify as Min, an ithyphallic fertility god depicted seated with erect phallus and upraised flail, approached by a serpent — is labeled by Smith 'God sitting upon his throne, revealing through the heavens the grand Key-words of the Priesthood; as, also, the sign of the Holy Ghost unto Abraham, in the form of a dove.' Even LDS scholar Michael Rhodes's translation of the hypocephalus rim and panels yields standard funerary formulae for Sheshonq, not Abrahamic cosmology; portions of the original were missing and were filled in for the 1842 publication with characters copied from other papyri (including lines from the Hor Book of Breathings).
bom: Book of Abraham, Facsimile 2 Explanation, Figs. 1, 5, 7

sources.name: Ritner, The Joseph Smith Egyptian Papyri: A Complete Edition (2013) — hypocephalus translation; summarized with images
BYU Studies / Pearl of Great Price Central: 'God Sitting upon His Throne (Facsimile 2, Figure 7)' — concedes the figure is Min
FAIR: Facsimile 2 — identification of the ithyphallic god Min as 'God sitting upon his throne'
Gospel Topics essay: 'Translation and Historicity of the Book of Abraham' (LDS Church)

response: LDS scholarship (Rhodes, Gee, Muhlestein; Pearl of Great Price Central) concedes figure 7 depicts a form of Min but argues: (1) Min was for Egyptians a supreme creator-god symbolizing regenerative, procreative power — so 'God sitting upon his throne' captures the figure's functional meaning within Egyptian religion even if the iconography shocks modern readers; (2) hypocephali were esoteric objects encoding cosmic geography and rebirth, so a cosmological reading is not categorically alien to the genre, and a few of Smith's identifications (e.g., fig. 1 associated with the creative force at the center; fig. 4 as expanse/firmament, a ship figure some Egyptologists relate to the sky-journey) are argued to land near Egyptian concepts; (3) under the Semitic-adaptation and catalyst frameworks, Smith's explanations were never meant as Egyptological decipherment but as inspired repurposing, paralleling how Egyptian Jews reused pagan iconography.

responseSource.name: Pearl of Great Price Central: God Sitting Upon His Throne (Facsimile 2, Figure 7)

rationale: There is no dispute about what figure 7 is — apologetic sources themselves identify it as ithyphallic Min. The dispute is only whether 'God sitting upon his throne, revealing the grand Key-words of the Priesthood... the sign of the Holy Ghost... in the form of a dove' can be rescued as a functional-equivalence reading of a pagan fertility figure being approached by a serpent. No Egyptologist reads the hypocephalus as teaching Kolob, priesthood key-words, or the Holy Ghost; Rhodes's own faithful translation of the object's actual text yields conventional funerary petitions for Sheshonq. The steelman does not counter the translation evidence; it relocates Smith's explanations outside translation entirely — which concedes the empirical point while contesting its theological weight. Under a Deut 18 / 1 Thess 5:21 test of a man who claimed to translate 'by the gift and power of God,' the specific, checkable claims fail checking and remain unrefuted by any counter-translation.

title: Facsimile 3: Readable Captions Name the Figures — and Contradict Every Smith Label
claim: Facsimile 3 is a standard 'presentation' vignette from the Book of Breathings of the priest Hor: the deceased Hor, led by Maat and Anubis, presented before the enthroned Osiris with Isis behind him. Unlike Facsimile 1, the hieroglyphic captions above/beside each figure survive in the published woodcut and name the figures, and Egyptologists can read them. Robert Ritner's translations: fig. 2 (which Smith labeled 'King Pharaoh, whose name is given in the characters above his head') is captioned 'Isis the great, the god's mother' — a goddess; fig. 4 (Smith: 'Prince of Pharaoh, King of Egypt, as written above the hand') is 'Maat, mistress of the gods' — also a goddess; fig. 1 (Smith: 'Abraham sitting upon Pharaoh's throne') is the god Osiris; fig. 5 (Smith: 'Shulem, one of the king's principal waiters') is captioned 'The Osiris Hor, justified forever' — the papyrus owner himself; fig. 6 (Smith: 'Olimlah, a slave belonging to the prince') is the god Anubis. Smith thus rendered two female goddesses as male royalty and claimed their names were 'given in the characters above' — characters that, once read, name Isis and Maat. Earlier Egyptologists shown the facsimiles (Deveria 1860, and the 1912 panel including Petrie and Breasted) reached the same conclusions independently.

sources.name: Ritner, The Joseph Smith Egyptian Papyri: A Complete Edition (2013) — Facsimile 3 caption translations; quoted in FAIR's treatment
FAIR: responses to Joseph Smith's interpretations of Facsimile 3 (quotes Ritner, Parker, Baer readings)
Pearl of Great Price Central: 'Isis the Pharaoh (Facsimile 3, Figure 2)'
Gospel Topics essay: 'Translation and Historicity of the Book of Abraham' (LDS Church)
Book of Abraham Facsimile 3 analysis with caption images (4witness)

response: The strongest apologetic (Gee, Muhlestein, Pearl of Great Price Central) does not offer a rival translation of the captions; it accepts the Egyptological readings and argues reidentification: (1) in Egyptian theology Pharaoh was understood as the earthly embodiment of Osiris, and Isis could be ritually identified with the (female-titled) throne and even with the king — so 'Isis as Pharaoh' has attested conceptual precedent; (2) ancient Semitic peoples demonstrably adapted Egyptian vignettes for their own figures (Jewish reuse of Egyptian iconography, Abraham appearing in later Egyptian magical texts), so an ancient Jewish redactor could have relabeled this scene as an Abraham-at-court illustration; (3) presentation scenes involve dressing figures in others' iconography, so gender-crossing identifications are not unknown in Egyptian ritual texts; (4) some caption glyphs (notably the Isis name group) are poorly copied in the woodcut, complicating certainty about what stood on the original.

responseSource.name: Pearl of Great Price Central: Isis the Pharaoh (Facsimile 3, Figure 2)

rationale: This is the hardest facsimile case for the LDS position because Smith explicitly staked his labels on the characters themselves — 'whose name is given in the characters above his head' — and those characters, now readable, name Isis and Maat, not any Pharaoh or prince, and name the papyrus owner Hor where Smith saw 'Shulem the waiter.' No apologetic source produces a counter-translation; the Semitic-adaptation steelman concedes the Egyptology and posits an undocumented ancient relabeling for which no direct evidence exists on this papyrus. The church's own essay concedes Egyptologists' interpretations do not match Smith's but stops short of conceding error, so the verdict is unrefuted rather than admitted. As a directly checkable translation claim made in the name of the gift and power of God, it fails the 1 Thess 5:21 / Deut 18 test on the evidence as it stands.
